Ethiopia's New Political Chapter - Sovereign Sea Access At the Heart of National Ambition
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia's New Political Chapter - Sovereign Sea Access At the Heart of National Ambition - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia's New Political Chapter - Sovereign Sea Access At the Heart of National Ambition 15 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Ethiopia's new five-year political chapter opens with a defining national ambition: building a peaceful, democratic and prosperous state while pursuing sovereign access to the sea. Under the Medemer Government, the government is highly anticipated to translating its electoral mandate into tangible improvements in citizens' lives while strengthening Ethiopia's strategic position in the Horn of Africa. At the heart of this agenda lies Ethiopia's sovereign sea access aspiration. As one of the world's most populous landlocked countries, Ethiopia has a compelling economic interest in reliable access to maritime trade. Securing such access through mutually beneficial arrangements could ease logistical constraints, improve export competitiveness, attract investment and deepen regional economic integration. Yet, maritime access is part of a broader national transformation. The success of Ethiopia's new political chapter will depend equally on consolidating peace, strengthening democratic institutions, advancing national reconciliation and building an inclusive economy. The Medemer philosophy, which emphasizes cooperation, synergy and collective progress, offers a framework for pursuing these priorities. Its credibility will ultimately rest on the government's ability to translate political commitments into measurable results. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Ethiopia's domestic progress also carries regional significance. As host of the African Union headquarters and a major political and economic actor in the Horn of Africa, the country has both a strategic interest in regional stability and an opportunity to contribute to it. A stronger Ethiopia, supported by trusted institutions and a resilient economy, would be better positioned to advance its national interests while promoting peace and cooperation across the region. Sovereign Sea Access: A Strategic National Priority For Ethiopia, access to the sea is more than a question of geography. It is closely connected to security, trade, economic competitiveness, national development and long-term strategic interests. Dependence on external maritime corridors exposes the country's economy to transport costs, logistical bottlenecks and disruptions in international trade. Reliable and diversified access to maritime infrastructure could help Ethiopian businesses reach international markets more efficiently, strengthen supply chains and improve the competitiveness of exports. Ethiopia must be an integral part of the Red Sea security architecture. As a major regional actor with longstanding contributions to peacekeeping under the United Nations and peace and security efforts across the Horn of Africa, Ethiopia has a compelling strategic interest in the security of this vital maritime corridor and a meaningful contribution to make. Excluding a country of Ethiopia's regional significance from decisions affecting Red Sea security would leave a critical stakeholder outside a process with direct implications for its economic and national interests. Ethiopia should therefore have a meaningful seat at the table, enabling it to contribute to maritime security, protect international shipping, strengthen regional stability and help safeguard one of the world's most strategically important waterways. Ultimately, the measure of progress will be whether Ethiopia can expand its maritime options, reduce trade constraints and strengthen its economic resilience while contributing to stability across the Horn of Africa. National Unity as Foundation of Strategic Ambition No national ambition can be sustained without internal stability and a shared sense of purpose. Ethiopia's new political chapter must therefore begin with the responsibility to strengthen national unity, address longstanding grievances and rebuild public confidence. The country's cultural diversity, complex history and competing political interests make inclusive state building essential. Unity cannot be achieved through declarations alone. It requires equal citizenship, constitutional protection, fair access to opportunities and institutions capable of managing disagreements peacefully. The Medemer approach can help create common ground among political parties, government institutions, civil society organizations, religious institutions, traditional leaders and communities. The national dialogue process offers an opportunity to address historical grievances, identify shared interests and build a stronger foundation for consensus. For this process to succeed, participation must be meaningful, diverse perspectives must be heard, and recommendations must inform practical reforms. National reconciliation should not be reduced to a political slogan; it must produce greater trust, improved relations among communities and more effective mechanisms for resolving disputes. Democratic Institutions: Turning the Mandate into Public Trust The durability of Ethiopia's political transition will depend heavily on the performance of its democratic institutions. Parliament, the judiciary, electoral bodies and executive institutions must operate within their constitutional mandates and provide effective mechanisms for accountability. The House of Peoples' Representatives has a responsibility not only to enact legislation but also to scrutinize government performance, examine public expenditure and ensure that national policies respond to citizens' needs. Effective parliamentary oversight can help identify implementation gaps, improve public spending and strengthen accountability. An independent and accessible judiciary is equally important. Citizens must be able to seek remedies when their rights are violated, while disputes should be resolved through impartial legal procedures. Consistent application of the law would reinforce equal protection and improve confidence in public institutions. Political parties also have a responsibility to strengthen democratic practices by presenting credible policy alternatives, engaging in constructive debate and respecting constitutional procedures. The government, in turn, must protect lawful political participation, civic engagement and public criticism. Combating corruption, reducing administrative inefficiency and improving public services are equally important. Transparent procurement, responsible financial management and accessible complaint mechanisms would help ensure that public resources serve their intended purposes. These reforms are directly connected to Ethiopia's broader strategic ambitions. Predictable institutions and accountable governance can strengthen investor confidence, improve the business environment and support the effective implementation of infrastructure and development projects. A government that earns public trust at home is also better positioned to build credible partnerships abroad. Democratic accountability is therefore not separate from national strategy; it is one of the foundations on which sustainable national progress depends. Economic Transformation and Building the Capacity for Sovereignty Ethiopia's pursuit of sea access must be supported by an economy capable of turning improved connectivity into prosperity. Access to ports and international markets can create opportunities, but the benefits will depend on domestic productivity, competitive industries and the capacity to generate value. In this regard, Ethiopia's "Made in Ethiopia" industrial movement is playing an important role in strengthening domestic production, advancing import substitution and expanding the country's manufacturing capacity. By encouraging local industries to produce goods previously sourced from abroad, the initiative supports economic self-reliance, reduces import dependence and creates opportunities for domestic investment and job creation. Agriculture remains central to Ethiopia's food security and economy. Under the Medemer philosophy, the country has made notable progress, particularly in wheat production. Expanding irrigation, mechanization, research and agro-processing can further boost productivity, reduce climate vulnerability and increase farmers' incomes. Industrialization, manufacturing and digital transformation are equally vital to diversifying exports, creating jobs and strengthening domestic production. Reliable power, efficient logistics, access to finance and a skilled workforce will be essential to building competitive businesses. Improved maritime connectivity could lower trade barriers and connect Ethiopian producers to global markets, while stronger domestic industries would help the country capture greater value from international trade. Horn of Africa and Red Sea Region Cooperation for Shared Prosperity Ethiopia's national future is closely connected to developments across the Horn of Africa. Conflict, displacement, food insecurity and climate pressures frequently cross borders, while political tensions can disrupt trade and threaten the livelihoods of border communities. The pursuit of sea access must therefore be approached within a wider framework of regional cooperation. Ethiopia's strategic and economic interests must be connected to the Red Sea coast in the near future for mutual benefits. Port operations, transport corridors, logistics services and cross-border infrastructure can create commercial opportunities for participating countries. Improved connectivity can strengthen regional supply chains, expand markets and encourage investment in transport, manufacturing and trade-related services. A more stable and connected Horn of Africa would benefit Ethiopia's maritime aspirations while supporting the development priorities of its neighbors. Ethiopia's regional influence will therefore depend not only on the scale of its ambitions but also on its ability to build trust, sustain dialogue and demonstrate that cooperation can deliver tangible benefits. Climate Resilience and Water Security on Nile River Equally important to Ethiopia's ambition for sovereign sea access, the new Medemer Government must maximize the development potential of the Abay (Blue Nile) River by advancing additional hydropower and irrigation projects. Harnessing this strategic resource is vital to expanding electricity generation, strengthening food security and accelerating economic transformation. Climate resilience remains central to this ambition. Droughts, floods and shifting rainfall patterns threaten agriculture, water supplies, infrastructure and livelihoods across the Horn of Africa. Ethiopia's investment in hydropower and irrigation must therefore go hand in hand with sustainable water management, environmental protection and climate adaptation. For Ethiopia, maximizing the Abay River's potential is not merely an energy or irrigation priority; it is a strategic pillar of economic sovereignty, food security and long-term national development. Youth and Women: Expanding the Foundations of National Progress Ethiopia's young population represents a major opportunity for economic growth, innovation and national renewal. Realizing this potential requires more than expanding education; it demands relevant skills, productive employment, entrepreneurship and meaningful participation in public life. Limited employment opportunities can deepen frustration, particularly when young people feel excluded from decisions affecting their future. Investment in technical and vocational education, digital skills and employment-intensive sectors would help connect education with the needs of the economy. Stronger links between schools, universities, training institutions and employers could improve the transition from education to employment. Support for entrepreneurship and small businesses could also enable young people to turn their skills and ideas into productive economic activity. Youth participation is equally important in national reconciliation, community development and public debate. Providing meaningful opportunities for young people to contribute to public affairs would strengthen social cohesion and ensure that national policies respond to their priorities. Women's participation is another essential component of inclusive development. Expanding access to education, employment, finance, public services and leadership would allow more citizens to contribute to national progress and strengthen household welfare. These investments have strategic significance. A skilled, productive and economically empowered population would strengthen domestic industries, improve export competitiveness and help Ethiopia benefit from expanded regional and international trade. National ambition becomes more sustainable when citizens have a genuine stake in its realization. Empowering young people and women is therefore not simply a social objective; it is an investment in Ethiopia's productive capacity, stability and long-term prosperity. From National Ambition to Measurable Results The credibility of Ethiopia's new political chapter will ultimately depend on implementation. The government must translate its priorities into clear targets, allocate resources according to national needs and establish mechanisms for assessing progress. Security, employment, public service delivery, institutional accountability and economic resilience should be central measures of performance. Federal and regional authorities must coordinate their responsibilities while respecting constitutional mandates and local circumstances. Consultation with communities, businesses, professional associations and civil society can improve decision-making and help identify emerging problems. Efficient public financial management, stronger procurement systems and effective anti-corruption measures would help ensure that limited resources deliver meaningful results. The government must also balance long-term infrastructure investments with immediate public needs. Citizens expect improved access to health care, education, affordable food, employment and personal security. Progress in these areas will shape public confidence in the administration. Strategic ambitions and domestic responsibilities should reinforce each other. Maritime access can expand economic opportunities and its full value should depend on productive industries, capable institutions, skilled workers and a stable political environment. The ultimate test is whether national policies improve the lives of citizens while strengthening Ethiopia's ability to pursue its interests through peaceful and constructive engagement. All in all, Ethiopia's new five-year political chapter presents an opportunity to strengthen the foundations of a peaceful, democratic and prosperous state. Its success will depend on the government's ability to translate its electoral mandate and the Medemer philosophy into tangible progress in national unity, security, institutional accountability and living standards. At the heart of the country's strategic ambition is sovereign access to the sea. Pursued through mutually beneficial arrangements, maritime connectivity could help ease trade constraints, strengthen export competitiveness and deepen regional economic integration as well as ensure lasting peace. Beyond its borders, Ethiopia must strengthen constructive relations with neighboring states, advance cooperation on trade, infrastructure, energy and climate resilience, and support regional efforts to prevent conflict. Its engagement with the African Union and IGAD can help advance these goals when backed by consistent diplomacy and practical commitments. The government's responsibility is therefore both national and regional: to build a state that citizens trust, an economy that expands opportunities and a foreign policy that advances national interests while respecting the legitimate interests of others. Sovereign access to the sea may be at the heart of Ethiopia's national ambition, but national unity, democratic governance and economic transformation will determine its success. The defining measure of the Medemer State will be its ability to turn this ambition into lasting improvements in citizens' lives while contributing to a more peaceful, stable and economically integrated Horn of Africa. ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Seeking Renewable Energy Investment, Stronger Public-Private Partnerships
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Seeking Renewable Energy Investment, Stronger Public-Private Partnerships - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia Seeking Renewable Energy Investment, Stronger Public-Private Partnerships 15 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Ethiopia is seeking increased investment and stronger public-private partnerships to expand renewable energy use and support agricultural productivity, business growth and improved livelihoods. The ongoing Second Ethiopian Renewable Energy Summit 2026 which opened today focuses on attracting investment, expanding energy access and strengthening the contribution of renewable energy to the country's economic development. Water and Energy Minister Habtamu Iteffa, through his representative, noted that electric power is essential for economic transformation, industrial development, public services, agricultural productivity and improved living standards. Therefore, Ethiopia needs to expand its national grid while complementing it with decentralized renewable energy solutions, including solar home systems, mini-grids and technologies that enable businesses and communities to use energy productively. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn "Our objective must be to move from dialogue to investments, from isolated initiatives to scale-up solutions, and from commitments to implementation," he said. The Minister also underscored the importance of private-sector participation in the energy transition through capital investment, technical expertise, innovation, distribution networks, job creation and local manufacturing. He said expanding the market requires a predictable policy and regulatory environment, access to finance and foreign exchange, quality standards and business models that make renewable energy solutions affordable and sustainable. Agriculture Minister Addisu Arega, through his representative, highlighted the role of renewable energy in improving agricultural production, addressing climate-related challenges and strengthening farmers' resilience to irregular rainfall and rising production costs. He said solar-powered irrigation can improve farmers' access to water, reduce dependence on diesel-powered pumps and support crop diversification. Renewable energy can also power cold storage, refrigerated transport and other facilities that help preserve agricultural products and reduce post-harvest losses. Moreover, renewable energy can support agricultural processing, dairy production, rural water supply, veterinary services, digital agriculture and access to agricultural inputs. However, high upfront costs, limited access to affordable finance, gaps in technical skills and challenges in equipment maintenance remain barriers to wider adoption. Addisu emphasized the need for stronger public-private partnerships, technical training, affordable financing and coordinated planning across the agriculture, water and energy sectors to ensure that renewable energy technologies meet the needs of farmers and rural communities. For her part, Ethiopian Solar Energy Development Association (ESEDA) General Manager Yemissirach Sisay said the summit seeks to demonstrate the readiness and capacity of private companies to contribute to Ethiopia's energy transition and turn the country's renewable energy potential into practical results. "The private sector is not waiting on the sidelines of national development," she noted. The General Manager highlighted opportunities in solar-powered water pumps for smallholder farmers, mini-grids for communities without adequate electricity access, clean cooking technologies and sustainable electric mobility. Addressing investment risks, foreign exchange constraints, taxation and financing challenges would help local companies expand from small-scale distribution to larger renewable energy projects. Yemissirach also stressed the importance of cooperation among African renewable energy associations to share experience, improve regulatory coordination, expand regional trade and support the development of a more integrated African energy market. The summit has brought together representatives of the government, renewable energy companies, private-sector investors, financial institutions, development partners and other stakeholders The summit, which runs up to 17 October 2026, provides a platform for collaboration and investment in the renewable energy sector. ethiopia.title: Egyptian Analyst Rebukes Egypt's Leaders for Trying to Block Ethiopia's Sovereign Right to Red Sea
ethiopia.content: Egyptian Analyst Rebukes Egypt's Leaders for Trying to Block Ethiopia's Sovereign Right to Red Sea - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Egyptian Analyst Rebukes Egypt's Leaders for Trying to Block Ethiopia's Sovereign Right to Red Sea 15 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — The Egyptian political analyst Magdi Khalil has strongly criticized the leaders of Egypt for opposing and fighting Ethiopia's right of access to the Red Sea. "If there were leaders in Egypt with vision and foresight, they would work to help Ethiopia gain access to the Red Sea instead of opposing and fighting it," he said. The Egyptian analyst criticized the country's opposition to Ethiopia's efforts to secure access to the Red Sea and called on Egypt to reassess its policy toward Ethiopia and shift from confrontation to cooperation. In a Zoom interview with ENA, Khalil said that Ethiopia, as a large landlocked country, has the sovereign right to gain access to the Red Sea. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn "Ethiopia has the sovereign right to conclude agreements with countries to secure one or more outlets on the Red Sea, provided this is done peacefully, whether for fifty or one hundred years," he added. The analyst further questioned the reasons behind opposition to Ethiopia's access to the Red Sea, noting that Ethiopia's historical coastal presence had not been a source of harm to neighboring countries. Ethiopia's demands should therefore be addressed through cooperation and mutual interests rather than political confrontation and hostility. Khalil called for a meeting involving the countries bordering the Red Sea to discuss shared interests and reach regional understandings. The Egyptian analyst stressed the importance of replacing hostile competition with cooperation, emphasizing that peaceful agreements could provide a practical framework for addressing Ethiopia's maritime needs. According to him, some countries were willing to reach agreements with Ethiopia to provide maritime access, arguing that long-term arrangements could strengthen cooperation and stability in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea region. Furthermore, Khalil criticized Egypt's historical position on the Eritrean issue, noting that Egypt, alongside other Arab countries, participated in supporting the Eritrean Liberation Front, which was established in Cairo in 1960. He argued that Eritrea's independence in 1991 and Ethiopia's subsequent landlocked status necessitate a reassessment of the regional positions that contributed to this situation. The analyst described Egypt's support for the Eritrean movement as a historical mistake that harmed relations that should have been based on cooperation between the two countries. ethiopia.title: Somaliland President Rejects Interference Threatening Ethiopia's Security
ethiopia.content: Somalia: Somaliland President Rejects Interference Threatening Ethiopia's Security - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Somalia: Somaliland President Rejects Interference Threatening Ethiopia's Security 15 October 2026 Horn Diplomat (Hargeisa) By Mohamed Duale Hargeisa — Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdillahi said on Thursday that Somaliland strongly opposed interference and any actions that could threaten neighbouring Ethiopia's stability and security. Speaking at the presidential palace in Hargeisa after returning from visits to the United States and the United Arab Emirates, Abdillahi, widely known as Irro, expressed firm support for Ethiopia's security. "We strongly oppose interference and any act that could endanger Ethiopia's stability and security," he said. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines His remarks followed diplomatic and military engagements between Somaliland and Ethiopia this week, alongside Somaliland's renewed willingness to discuss maritime access for its landlocked neighbour. Foreign Minister Abdirahman Dahir Adan Bakal said in an interview with Sky News Arabia , reported on Monday, that Somaliland was ready to discuss Ethiopian access to its coastline and Berbera port. He described Ethiopia as a close ally and urged dialogue to resolve regional disputes. Ethiopian Ambassador Teshome Shunde separately met Bakal and Somaliland army chief Brigadier General Nimcan Yusuf Gahnuug i n Hargeisa. According to statements from Somaliland's foreign ministry and military, the discussions covered bilateral relations, defence cooperation and regional security, with both sides emphasising cooperation to support peace and stability. Somaliland and Ethiopia maintain close ties spanning trade, security and diplomatic engagement. Their shared border and economic links make stability in the region an important interest for both sides. ethiopia.title: Can Ethiopia Ever Be At Peace? Four Reasons Conflict Keeps Flaring Up
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Can Ethiopia Ever Be At Peace? Four Reasons Conflict Keeps Flaring Up - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Can Ethiopia Ever Be At Peace? Four Reasons Conflict Keeps Flaring Up 15 October 2026 The Conversation Africa (Johannesburg) analysis By Alemayehu Fentaw Weldemariam Ethiopia has experienced recurrent conflicts for over five decades. This includes a long-running civil war sparked by the overthrow of Emperor Haile Selassie in 1974, renewed fighting in Tigray, and ongoing conflicts in Amhara and Oromia . The renewed hostilities in Tigray threaten to undo a peace process that had begun with an agreement signed in Pretoria, South Africa, in 2022. Why has peace been so difficult to sustain in Ethiopia? My research on constitutional design and conflict points to four interconnected explanations: the foundations of the Ethiopian state remain contested ceasefires are mistaken for political settlements armed force continues to be a route to political power regional rivalries reinforce internal conflicts. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The problem isn't that Ethiopians of diverse ethnic backgrounds hate one another and can't live together peacefully. It's that successive political arrangements have failed to establish widely accepted rules for managing disagreements. 1. The foundations of the state remain contested Ethiopia's 1995 constitution emerged from a political transition that followed the overthrow of the military government in 1991. This ended nearly two decades of civil war . The new leadership sought to address long-standing grievances over ethnic marginalisation and demands for greater autonomy. It restructured the country as a federation largely organised around ethnolinguistic communities. The constitution vested sovereignty in Ethiopia's nations, nationalities and peoples. It guaranteed their right to self-determination, including secession . Proponents of federalism regard this right as protection against historical domination. Opponents argue that it entrenches ethnic boundaries and encourages competition over territory and resources . Ethnic diversity doesn't inevitably lead to violence. And federalism isn't inherently destabilising. It was introduced to accommodate competing national claims within a common political order. But constitutional recognition is not the same as political reconciliation. Read more: What is federalism? Why Ethiopia uses this system of government and why it's not perfect The problem arises when a constitution sets out rules for sharing power and governing the country without sufficient agreement among the political groups expected to follow them. Instead of providing a common framework for resolving disputes, those rules become another source of political conflict . 2. Ceasefires are mistaken for political settlements The 2022 Pretoria agreement was about stopping hostilities, not about resolving their causes. The federal government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front agreed to end two years of war. Major political questions were left for later negotiation. Disputed territories, regional administration, political participation and accountability for wartime abuses remain contentious . Eritrea, a major participant in the 2020-2022 war in Tigray, did not sign the agreement. Eritrean forces are still present in parts of Tigray. The Tigray People's Liberation Front itself also became fragmented after the war. Divisions emerged within the leadership. Disagreements over federal relations, political authority and control of military forces developed into a struggle within the movement. A peace agreement assumes that the parties signing it have authority over their political and military organisations to honour their commitments. But when these organisations fragment, it becomes unclear who can carry out agreements. The Tigray leadership's loss of legal party status in 2025 added another obstacle to political reintegration. These developments have undermined confidence that the transition from armed conflict to constitutional politics would be honoured. Read more: Ethiopia's peace deal is unravelling - what went wrong with the Tigray agreement This distinction is fundamental. A cessation of hostilities can save lives immediately. But it cannot, by itself, establish a legitimate regional government, resolve territorial claims or restore trust between former enemies. 3. Armed force is a route to political power The use of violence to acquire or retain political authority has deep roots in Ethiopia's modern history. In 1974 , the military overthrew the empire-state and established a military regime. This regime was itself overthrown in 1991 by a coalition of rebel forces led by the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front. These transitions reinforced a pattern in which political power could be won through armed struggle. When political opponents have little confidence that elections, courts or negotiations can bring change, taking up arms can appear more effective than peaceful political competition. The continued use of force by both the state and armed groups makes this cycle difficult to break . Read more: Ethiopia's national dialogue was meant to heal the nation, but divisions are deepening Abiy Ahmed became prime minister in 2018 after years of anti-government protests and divisions within the ruling coalition. Two years later, rising political tensions led to war in Tigray. Abiy's regime has faced accusations of serious rights abuses and a lack of accountability. This has deepened distrust. It's made negotiated settlements harder to achieve. Under Abiy, political authority has become increasingly personalised. Military operations and extraordinary security measures have been used to confront political challenges. Peace needs a political environment where losing an election doesn't mean exclusion from power or exposure to coercion. 4. Regional rivalries reinforce internal conflicts Ethiopia's domestic conflicts are increasingly intersecting with the interests and actions of neighbouring countries. Eritrean forces fought beside Ethiopia's army in Tigray. They remained in parts of the region after the 2022 peace deal. Now the former allies are adversaries . There have been accusations of cross-border military intervention . This has renewed concerns that the war in Tigray could develop into a wider conflict. Ethiopia's ambitions to secure Red Sea access have further complicated relations with Eritrea and Somalia. Its 2024 agreement with Somaliland provoked a dispute with Mogadishu. Ethiopia also has strained relations with Egypt over its mega dam in the Nile River . Sudan's ongoing civil war and rival Saudi Arabia and Emirati relationships across the Red Sea add further pressures . Read more: Ethiopia and Eritrea are on edge again: what's behind the growing risk of war These external tensions can make domestic troubles harder to contain. Ethiopia has a duty to defend its boundaries and also to respect those of its neighbours. What would lasting peace require? These four obstacles to peace reinforce one another: disagreements over constitutional rules fuel political tensions armed conflict makes inclusive negotiations more difficult peace agreements that fail to address underlying grievances leave the door open to renewed violence competing regional interests complicate efforts to achieve lasting peace. As a result, Ethiopia's recurring conflicts cannot be resolved through ceasefires alone. Lasting peace requires all Ethiopians to agree on how power is shared, and the relationship between the federal government and its regions. Read more: What makes peace talks successful? The 4 factors that matter But resolving Ethiopia's internal divisions will not, on its own, settle tensions with neighbouring countries. That requires diplomacy built on respect for sovereignty, non-interference and peaceful negotiation over interests. Ethiopia therefore faces two interconnected challenges. First, building a political system that its diverse communities can accept. Second, establishing peaceful relations with its neighbours. Lasting peace depends on both.
